title: Guru Har Krishan: healing
hookLine: the eighth Guru's light: the child who served the sick
tomorrow: why would a Guru die for a faith that wasn't his own?

lines: A CHILD GURU AMONG THE SICK.
cards: Baba Kartar has a cough that won't quit, and he's decided not to see a doctor. Suffering is the medicine, he says, quoting the Granth, and goes back to his tea. Harjit says he's being stubborn.
Simran is caught in the middle, texting you from the hallway. And the Guru for this argument is a child.
Tradition says Guru Har Krishan became Guru very young, and when he came to Delhi, sickness was moving through the city. He went among the sick and served them, caught the illness himself, and died.
A hard story, told gently: he gave his short life to people who were ill.

teach.b: Here's the line Baba Kartar quoted, from Guru Nanak in Asa di Var, Ang 469. In paraphrase: suffering is the medicine, and comfort the disease, because in comfort we forget.
Readers take it two ways, and both love the line.
One side says: take it as it stands. Pain teaches what comfort hides; meet it without bitterness and let it turn you toward the Name.
Its best case: the line isn't about doctors at all, and someone who has learned from pain has learned something real.
The other side says: read it beside the Gurus' lives. Guru Har Rai kept medicines. Guru Har Krishan, still a child, walked toward the sick.
Its best case: the line is about pride and forgetting, not refusing care; accepting God's will can include accepting a doctor.
What both keep is the Ardas, which remembers him like this, in paraphrase: think of Guru Har Krishan, and seeing him, all suffering goes.
One to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh standing prayer remembers a child Guru as a healer. Simran doesn't win the argument.
She sits with Baba Kartar and says: the child Guru went to the sick. Maybe the sick can go to the doctor. He laughs, coughs, and says he'll think about it.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan in the Ardas as the one whose sight removes suffering; Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi, linked with his stay there, is visited by many, and its sarovar water is taken home by some.

o: a healer saint whose herbs are named in the Granth
the eighth Guru, a child who served the sick and caught it
the Guru who wrote the hymns of the morning prayer

s: 'suffering is the medicine' tells Sikhs to refuse doctors

the Ardas remembers Guru Har Krishan as one whose sight removes suffering

games.q: your aunt quotes 'suffering is the medicine' to argue her friend shouldn't take pain medicine after surgery. what's the other side's best case?
o: the line is about pride and forgetting; the Gurus themselves went toward healing.
the line was only meant for Guru Nanak's own time, before modern doctors.
pain medicine shows weak faith, so the line doesn't apply to her.
games.why: the steelman: the Gurus kept medicines and served the sick. the line warns against forgetting in comfort, not against care.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's unwell right now, in body or in spirit. Write them a short message, just a few honest words, and leave it ready on your screen.
Breathe slowly with their name in mind, and when the sit ends, decide whether to send it.

wordCard.voice: Guru Har Krishan: the eighth Guru, a child who went toward the sick. Healing, given at a cost.
